note: Unit sets are data, not code. flyto_robotics.lifecycle renders whatever this
file declares and never names a transport, a middleware, or a robot vendor.
A customer running something other than ROS 2 adds a profile here (or points
--profiles at their own file) and gets the identical install/update/rollback
commands. `extends` keeps an added profile purely additive: the base units
must render byte-identically in every profile that extends it, otherwise
adopting a profile would silently rewrite the units a site already runs.
Template fields are substituted from flyto_robotics.lifecycle.Layout:
current, config_dir, config_file, state_dir, log_dir, python.
enable  -- `systemctl enable` it so it survives a reboot
restart -- `systemctl restart` it when a release is activated
verify  -- require `systemctl is-active` to report active afterwards

generic.description: Transport-agnostic base. No middleware, no vendor, no ROS.

readiness.description: the active release carries the package every ExecStart executes
note: Not provisioning: a release whose contents cannot satisfy its own units is
the release failing on this device, and is what the transaction undoes.

readiness.description: the configuration file the units read exists
the device has been given an identity
the site has pointed this device at a cloud
the device has been given a resource id

units.name: flyto-robot-agent.service
template: # systemd reads the start rate limit from [Unit] only. Placed in [Service] it is
# accepted and ignored, which is how a unit reaches NRestarts in the hundreds.
# The release directory is reached through the stable `current` symlink, never
# through a versioned path: a unit that named a version would have to be
# rewritten on every update, and a rollback would leave it pointing at a
# release that is no longer active.
# Every input is a persistent path. The old ExecStart ran a developer entry
# point whose four required flags the unit never passed, so on a real device it
# exited 2 on every start and Restart=on-failure turned that into a rate-limited
# loop that is-active reported as coming up. --profile is deliberately absent:
# `extends` requires this unit to render byte-identically in every profile that
# inherits it, so it may not name one.

units.name: flyto-robot-doctor.service
template: # robot_doctor has no --state-dir and requires --resource-id; the old command
# shape was an argparse usage error on every device in the fleet.

template: Description=Run the Flyto robot health snapshot every minute

This file is written by the installer and is never overwritten by a release.
Every command below is non-interactive, prints exactly one JSON object, and
exits 0 only when the operation actually succeeded.
flyto-robot status
What is installed, what is active, and what to do next.
flyto-robot install --from-package --version <V>
First install. Stages an immutable release, writes units, reloads
systemd, activates, and verifies the services came up. If anything
fails the device is left with nothing half-installed.
flyto-robot update --from-package --version <V>
Same operation, on a device that already runs something. If the new
release fails to start or fails its health check, the previous release
is restored automatically before the command returns.
flyto-robot rollback [--to-version <V>]
Return to the previously activated release, long after the fact.
flyto-robot support-bundle --output <FILE>
One redacted JSON file to attach to a ticket. It carries release
history, unit health, and file inventories. It never carries
credentials, identities, journals, Wi-Fi names, or addresses.
Every report has `reason` and `action_code`. Quote both when you open a
ticket; `action_code` says what to do without waiting for a reply.
Add --dry-run to install, update, or rollback to see exactly what would
change without writing anything at all.
